evidence.claim: Engineer William A. Welch developed the parkway proposal in 1933–34 to connect the New Jersey Palisades with parks farther north along the Hudson.
evidence.quote: In 1933–34, the first thoughts of a Palisades Interstate Parkway were developed by engineer and environmentalist William A. Welch

evidence.claim: John D. Rockefeller donated 700 acres in 1933, but the New Jersey Highway Commission’s opposition put the idea on hold.
evidence.quote: However, the New Jersey Highway Commission did not support construction, so the idea of a parkway was put on hold.

evidence.claim: Rockefeller renewed the campaign with Robert Moses in the 1940s, and construction began in New York in 1947.
evidence.quote: During the 1940s, Rockefeller renewed the push for a parkway along the New Jersey Palisades, and teamed with ultimate PIP planner, Robert Moses, to establish and design the parkway.

evidence.claim: to connect the New Jersey Palisades with parks farther north along the Hudson
evidence.quote: The plan was to build a parkway to connect the New Jersey Palisades with the state parks along the Hudson River in Rockland and Orange counties.

evidence.claim: Harriman’s lakes and roads owe part of their shape to public works during the Great Depression.
evidence.quote: The Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) offered thousands of young men work such as building roads, trails, camps and lakes.

evidence.claim: Civilian Conservation Corps crews built roads, trails and camps, and worked on lakes including Welch, Silvermine and Pine Meadow.
evidence.quote: Projects completed by the CCC in the park included Pine Meadow, Wanoksink, Turkey Hill, Welch, Silvermine and Massawippa Lakes.

evidence.claim: The park itself grew from Mary Harriman’s offer of 10,000 acres and $1 million in exchange for abandoning the state’s planned prison at Bear Mountain.
evidence.quote: Mary Harriman proposed to Governor Charles Evans Hughes that she would donate 10,000 acres (40 km2) of land and $1 million for the creation of a new state park.

evidence.claim: The state agreed, and the deed and check were presented in 1910.
evidence.quote: The state agreed and on October 29, 1910, Harriman's son W. Averell Harriman presented a deed for the land and a million-dollar check to the Commission.
